word: Lost Sheep of the House of Israel
pronunciation: LOST SHEEP uv thuh HOWS uv IZ-ray-el
pos: n. phr. (the covenant people to whom Christ was sent in the days of His flesh)
etymology: Greek ta probata ta apolōlota oikou Israēl — probaton, a sheep; apollumi in the perfect participle, having been lost or perished; the phrase renders a standing prophetic figure, Israel scattered because her shepherds fed themselves.
biblical_def: Twice in Matthew the Lord uses this phrase of the scope of His earthly mission. He charges the twelve, “Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into any city of the Samaritans enter ye not: But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” and He answers the Canaanite woman, “I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” The words are not a verdict on Gentiles but a statement of order. The promises were made to the fathers; the Messiah came first to His own; and the apostolic preaching afterwards went out from Jerusalem, to the Jew first and also to the Greek, exactly as the same Lord commanded when He sent the eleven to all nations. The figure itself is Ezekiel's. There the LORD indicts the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises to seek what was lost and to set one shepherd over them — and it is that promise Christ claims when He names Himself the good shepherd who giveth His life for the sheep and speaks of other sheep not of this fold whom He must also bring. The phrase therefore marks a sequence in redemptive history, not a boundary around the atonement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Lost, parted with; no longer possessed; wandered from the way. Sheep, a well-known ruminant; in Scripture, the people of God under His shepherding. The lost sheep of the house of Israel, Matthew 15:24, the covenant people Christ was first sent to seek.
webster_full: Lost, parted with unintentionally; no longer possessed; strayed from the way.
Sheep, a well-known ruminant animal; in Scripture, God's people under a shepherd.
House, in Scripture, a family, lineage, or nation descended from one head.
Greek apollūmi (perfect participle), having been lost, ruined, or perished.
Christ's answer to the woman of Canaan, Matthew 15:24.
scriptures: But he answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
Mat 10:6
But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but I will destroy the fat and the strong; I will feed them with judgment.
And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
corruption_summary: The phrase is pressed either into a racial restriction of Christ's saving work or into the dispensational claim that the kingdom offer was withdrawn from Israel and postponed.
corruption_paragraphs: British-Israelism and the Christian Identity movement that grew out of it take this verse as proof that Christ came for a bloodline, which they then assign to the nations of northern Europe and to no one else. The reading collapses on the same page. In the chapter where the Lord says He is not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, He goes on to heal the Canaanite woman's daughter and to commend her great faith; in the next book of the canon the Spirit falls on Cornelius's household; and Paul's letters make the dividing wall of partition broken down and the Gentiles fellowheirs of the same body. A gospel confined to a race is not the gospel of the apostles, and the ideology built on it is a genealogical fiction besides.

The dispensational construction errs differently. On that scheme Christ offered Israel an earthly kingdom, Israel refused, the offer was withdrawn, and the church age was inserted as an unforeseen parenthesis. Matthew's own narrative gives no such postponement: the same Gospel that records this saying ends with all nations commanded to be discipled, and Peter at Pentecost preaches that the promise is to the Jews and to their children and to all that are afar off. The Reformed reading keeps the one covenant of grace administered in stages, Christ coming first to the circumcision for the truth of God and the Gentiles brought in to glorify God for His mercy. The principle to recover is order without exclusion.
roots_summary: Greek probaton, sheep; apollūmi, to be lost or perish; oikos Israēl, the house of Israel — the figure taken from Ezekiel's indictment of the shepherds who scattered the flock.
roots_lines: Greek probaton, a sheep, the standing figure for God's dependent people.
Greek apollūmi, to destroy or lose; in the perfect, having been lost.
Greek oikos, a house, hence a household, lineage, or nation.
Drawn from Ezekiel 34, where the LORD seeks the flock His shepherds scattered.
Answered by other sheep not of this fold whom Christ must bring, John 10:16.
usage: But go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel
I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel
other sheep I have, which are not of this fold

pos: n. phr. (Christ's answer to a volunteer, naming His own homelessness)
etymology: Greek hai alōpekes phōleous echousin — alōpēx, a fox; phōleos, a den or lair; set against ouk echei pou tēn kephalēn klinē, hath not where to lay his head.
biblical_def: A scribe tells the Lord, Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest, and the answer is this: “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.” It is not a refusal and it is not self-pity. It is disclosure. The man has offered to go anywhere, and Christ tells him what anywhere means: a road with no house at the end of it, less shelter than a fox or a sparrow has by nature. The title He uses is deliberate — the Son of man, Daniel's figure of the one who receives an everlasting dominion, stands here without a roof. That is the poverty the apostle names when he says that though He was rich, yet for our sakes He became poor, and it belongs to His humiliation as truly as the manger and the borrowed tomb. Two things follow. First, the Lord deals honestly with volunteers; He never recruited a disciple by concealing the cost, and the next verses in both Matthew and Luke raise the price again rather than lowering it. Second, the homelessness is purposeful. He had not where to lay His head so that those who follow Him might have a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Fox, an animal of the genus Canis, remarkable for cunning. Hole, a hollow place; a cavern; the den of a wild beast. Foxes have holes, Matthew 8:20, Christ's word on His own homelessness to a would-be follower.
webster_full: Fox, an animal of the genus Canis, with a pointed nose, noted for cunning.
Hole, a hollow place; a cavern or pit; the burrow or den of a beast.
Greek alōpēx, a fox; also used by Christ of Herod, Luke 13:32.
Greek phōleos, a lurking-hole, den, or lair.
Set against the Son of man having nowhere to lay his head, Matthew 8:20.
scriptures: Mat 8:20
And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Luk 9:58
And Jesus said unto him, Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
Php 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
corruption_summary: The saying is turned into a general romance of poverty or an apostolic rule against property, when its subject is the particular humiliation of the Son of man and the honest cost of following Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Movements from the medieval mendicant orders to modern radical-discipleship writing have read this verse as establishing voluntary destitution as the higher Christian life, so that owning a house becomes a mark of compromise. Scripture does not legislate that way. The same Lord was entertained in houses at Bethany and Capernaum, Lydia and Philemon kept homes the church met in, and Paul tells Timothy that God giveth us richly all things to enjoy while commanding the rich to be ready to distribute. The verse is a statement about Christ's own condition and the cost of His particular itinerant call, not a universal rule turning property into sin.

The opposite drift is sentimental. Preached as a tender observation about a homeless teacher, the saying loses the thing it was said to do, which was to stop a man in his tracks and let him count. The Lord's dealings with volunteers are uniformly severe in this respect — he that taketh not his cross is not worthy of me, and whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself. The principle to recover is honest recruitment. A ministry that advertises comfort gathers followers the first hard providence will scatter, and the Son of man who had nowhere to lay His head told men the truth before they walked with Him.
roots_summary: Greek alōpēx, fox; phōleos, den; kataskenosis, a roosting place — creatures have shelter by nature; the Son of man, by His own choosing, had none.
roots_lines: Greek alōpēx, a fox, proverbial for cunning and for its earth or den.
Greek phōleos, a den or lair, the burrow a beast lies up in.
Greek kataskenosis, a lodging or roosting place, said of the birds of the air.
Greek klinō, to lay down or recline, hence nowhere to lay the head.
The title Son of man is Daniel's, Daniel 7:13, here without a roof.
usage: The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests
but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head
Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest

word: Let the Dead Bury Their Dead
pronunciation: let thuh DED BER-ee thair DED
pos: v. phr. (Christ's word to a disciple who asked leave to bury his father first)
etymology: Greek aphes tous nekrous thapsai tous heautōn nekrous — nekros, dead, used twice with two senses, the spiritually dead burying the naturally dead; aphiēmi, to leave or let alone.
biblical_def: “And another of his disciples said unto him, Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father. But Jesus said unto him, Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead.” The saying has struck readers as harsh in every generation, and its force depends on seeing that the one word dead is used in two senses. There are the dead to be buried, and there are the dead who may be left to bury them — men spiritually lifeless, able to perform the last offices of nature but not the first duty of grace. The request itself is weighty: burial of a father was a sacred filial charge in Israel, and the Lord elsewhere defends that commandment fiercely against the Pharisees' corban evasion. He is not abolishing the fifth commandment. He is settling an order of precedence when two claims collide and only one of them is the voice of God calling now. Luke adds the commission that makes the point plain: go thou and preach the kingdom of God. The verse that follows in Luke completes the lesson with the plough and the backward look. What Christ requires is not contempt for family but the refusal of first — suffer me first — since whatever a man puts before the call of Christ has become his master, however dutiful it looks.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Dead, deprived of life; also, in Scripture, spiritually dead, destitute of the life of grace. Bury, to inter a deceased person. Let the dead bury their dead, Matthew 8:22, the spiritually dead left to the offices of nature while the called man follows Christ.
webster_full: Dead, deprived of life; also in Scripture spiritually dead, void of grace.
Bury, to inter a deceased person; to perform the offices of a funeral.
Greek nekros, dead; used in both the natural and the spiritual sense.
Greek aphiēmi, to let alone, leave, permit, or send away.
Luke adds: go thou and preach the kingdom of God, Luke 9:60.
scriptures: Mat 8:22
But Jesus said unto him, Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead.
Luk 9:60
Jesus said unto him, Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God.
Mat 8:21
And another of his disciples said unto him, Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father.
Luk 9:62
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: The saying is used either to excuse neglect of family duty in the name of ministry, or softened by critics into evidence that the Gospels preserve a harshness the church must now outgrow.
corruption_paragraphs: Within the church the common abuse is to quote the verse as warrant for neglecting parents, spouse, or children because the work is urgent. The same Lord forbids exactly that. He convicts the Pharisees for using religious pretext to withhold support from father and mother, and the apostle writes that a man who provides not for his own house has denied the faith and is worse than an infidel — naming the care of widowed mothers as a first charge on their children. The verse concerns the moment of a particular call and the word first in the disciple's request, not a standing permission to let duty go.

From outside, the saying is treated as a hard remnant of a harsher age that a kinder Christianity should now put behind it. That judgment mistakes the speaker. The one who said this wept at a grave, provided for His mother from the cross, and raised a widow's only son on the way to his burial, which is the context Luke has just given. There is no cruelty in Him to outgrow. The principle to recover is the one the text actually presses: the claims of nature are real and good, and the call of Christ outranks them, so that a man may bury his father in faith but may not make the burying his reason for not following.
roots_summary: Greek nekros used twice in two senses, the spiritually dead and the naturally dead; aphiēmi, to leave alone; protōn, first, the word in the disciple's own request.
roots_lines: Greek nekros, dead; of the body in one clause, of the soul in the other.
Greek thaptō, to bury, to perform the funeral offices for the dead.
Greek aphiēmi, to let alone, leave, or permit to go their way.
Greek prōton, first — the word in ‘suffer me first’.
Luke pairs it with the hand on the plough and the backward look, Luke 9:62.
usage: Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead
Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father
go thou and preach the kingdom of God

pos: n. phr. (Christ's rebuke to Peter sinking on the water, after he had walked on it)
etymology: Greek oligopiste — a single compound vocative from oligos, little or few, and pistis, faith; the word is almost Christ's own, appearing in the New Testament only in His mouth.
biblical_def: Peter asked to come on the water, walked on it, saw the wind, was afraid, began to sink, and cried, Lord, save me. “And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?” The order of the sentence is the heart of it. The hand comes first and the rebuke after; the catching is not withheld until the faith improves. And the rebuke itself is precisely measured — little faith, not no faith, for the man had just walked on the sea at a word and his cry for rescue was itself an act of faith, rightly addressed. The word Christ uses here is one He uses of the anxious in the Sermon on the Mount and of the disciples in the storm and over the bread, always of true disciples whose faith is real and small. Scripture therefore gives us in this phrase a careful doctrine of weak faith: it is faith, it saves, it is rebuked, and it is held up by a hand stronger than itself. The Reformed divines made much of this against both presumption and despair, for a bruised reed is not broken, and he who prayed Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief was not sent away.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Little, small in quantity or degree; of small dignity or importance. Faith, the assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed; evangelical faith is the trust which the sinner reposes in Christ. O thou of little faith, Matthew 14:31, Christ's rebuke to a true but weak believer.
webster_full: Little, small in quantity, extent, or degree; not much.
Faith, the assent of the mind to what God reveals, with trust in Christ.
Greek oligopistos, of little faith, a compound used in the New Testament by Christ alone.
Greek distazō, to waver, hesitate, or be of two minds — ‘wherefore didst thou doubt?’
Spoken while holding Peter, after he had walked on the sea, Matthew 14:29-31.
scriptures: And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?
But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.
Mat 8:26
And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm.
Mar 9:24
And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
corruption_summary: The phrase is pressed into a doctrine of faith as a force whose quantity secures outcomes, so that failure is always the believer's fault and weak faith is treated as no faith at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The word-of-faith teaching makes faith a measurable power and this verse its proof text: Peter sank because he did not have enough, and the sick or poor believer is told the same of his own case. The passage will not carry it. What saved Peter was not a quantity of faith but the hand of Christ, stretched out immediately, and the faith that is commended elsewhere in the Gospels is repeatedly the size of a grain of mustard seed. Faith in Scripture is not a force a man generates and aims; it is a receiving, and its object does the work. Treating it as leverage turns the gospel into a technique and lays on sufferers a burden the apostles never laid.

The opposite error reads the rebuke as a verdict of unbelief and so teaches the weak to doubt whether they believe at all. Christ's own term forbids it: little faith is faith. The 1689 Confession allows that faith is different in degrees, weak or strong, may be often and many ways assailed and weakened, but gets the victory, growing up in many to the attainment of a full assurance. The principle to recover is pastoral and plain. A sinking disciple is to cry out as Peter did, and the hand that caught him is the same hand still, strong enough for small faith that calls on the right name.
roots_summary: Greek oligopistos, of little faith — oligos, little; pistis, faith; with distazō, to waver between two minds, the verb of the question that follows.
roots_lines: Greek oligos, little, small, or few in number or degree.
Greek pistis, faith, trust, or firm persuasion resting on another.
Greek oligopistos, of little faith, used only by Christ in the New Testament.
Greek distazō, to waver or stand in two minds, hence to doubt.
Spoken after the hand was already stretched out and holding, Matthew 14:31.
usage: O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?
Lord, save me
Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him

word: A Prophet Is Not Without Honour
pronunciation: uh PROF-et iz not with-OWT ON-ur
pos: n. phr. (Christ's word on His rejection at Nazareth, where familiarity bred offence)
etymology: Greek ouk estin prophētēs atimos ei mē en tēi patridi autou — atimos, unhonoured or held in no esteem, from the negative with timē, honour or price; patris, one's own country or native place.
biblical_def: At Nazareth they were astonished at His doctrine and then offended at His person — is not this the carpenter's son? — and the Lord replied, “A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.” Mark adds among his own kin, and Matthew records the consequence: He did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief. The saying states a rule that runs the length of Scripture. Joseph's brethren sold him; Moses was refused by the people he came to deliver; the prophets were stoned by Jerusalem; and John says simply that He came unto His own, and His own received Him not. The reason the Lord gives is not the prophet's failure but the hearers' familiarity. They knew the carpenter's shop, the mother, the brothers, and assumed that a man so thoroughly known could have nothing from God to say to them, which is unbelief wearing the dress of common sense. The warning falls on those nearest the means of grace. A town that had Christ in it for thirty years got less from Him than Capernaum did in a week, and churches long settled under faithful preaching are in the same danger of despising what they have grown used to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Prophet, one that foretells future events; also, one who speaks by divine inspiration. Honour, esteem due or paid to worth; reverence. A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, Matthew 13:57, Christ's word on the unbelief of the familiar.
webster_full: Prophet, one who speaks by divine inspiration, or foretells future events.
Honour, the esteem due to worth; respect, reverence, or high estimation.
Greek atimos, without honour, unhonoured, held of no price or esteem.
Greek patris, one's native country, fatherland, or home town.
Mark adds ‘among his own kin’, Mark 6:4; followed by unbelief, Matthew 13:58.
scriptures: And they were offended in him. But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house.
Mar 6:4
But Jesus said unto them, A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.
Luk 4:24
And he said, Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country.
Joh 1:11
He came unto his own, and his own received him not.
corruption_summary: The saying is taken up as a proverb excusing any rejected teacher, so that opposition itself becomes a credential and the test of true prophecy is quietly dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: In its commonest misuse the verse is quoted by a man whose message has been refused, as though being disbelieved at home proved him a prophet. It proves nothing of the kind. Scripture gives hard tests for a prophet — whether the word comes to pass, and more decisively whether it calls after other gods, in which case the sign may even come true and the prophet is still false — and the New Testament sets the apostolic doctrine as the standard by which every spirit is tried. The self-styled prophets of the New Apostolic Reformation use this saying to insulate their claims from examination, which is precisely the opposite of what the Bereans were commended for doing.

A second misreading flattens the saying into worldly wisdom about familiarity, as though Christ were observing that people undervalue what is close to hand. Matthew supplies the real category: it was unbelief, and the consequence was that mighty works were withheld. The principle to recover is therefore a warning rather than a proverb. The most dangerous place to sit is under long-familiar preaching, where the gospel has become ordinary; Nazareth heard the carpenter for thirty years and sent Him away, and a congregation can do the same thing slowly and politely.
roots_summary: Greek atimos, without honour or price; patris, one's own country; syngeneis, kin, added by Mark — and Matthew names the cause as unbelief, not the prophet's weakness.
roots_lines: Greek prophētēs, one who speaks forth the word of God.
Greek atimos, unhonoured, without esteem; from timē, honour or price.
Greek patris, one's native place, fatherland, or home town.
Greek syngeneis, kinsfolk, added in Mark's form of the saying.
The result at Nazareth was mighty works withheld, Matthew 13:58.
usage: A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country
Is not this the carpenter's son?
he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief

word: Where Two or Three Are Gathered
pronunciation: whair TOO or THREE ar GATH-erd
pos: n. phr. (Christ's promise of His presence with the assembly that acts in His name)
etymology: Greek hou gar eisin duo ē treis synēgmenoi eis to emon onoma — synagō in the perfect passive participle, having been gathered together; eis to emon onoma, into or unto My name, which is more than a label spoken over a meeting.
biblical_def: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” The promise is immense and its context is specific. It stands at the end of the Lord's instruction on discipline in the church: a brother is told his fault privately, then before two or three witnesses, then before the congregation; what the church binds on earth is bound in heaven; and the two or three who agree in asking are promised that it shall be done for them. The two or three are therefore not a minimum quorum for feeling God near but the witnesses and the assembly of Matthew's own paragraph, acting under Christ's authority in His name. Rightly read, the verse is one of the great texts for the local church. A small congregation discharging the Lord's own order has Christ in the midst of it — not less of Him than a multitude would have, for He is not divided by numbers — and the authority behind its discipline is heaven's. The baptist and congregational tradition has rested much here, and justly: the gathered church is Christ's institution and His presence is promised to it, which is why the apostle can speak of the power of our Lord Jesus Christ being present when the church is come together.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Gather, to bring together; to collect a number of separate things. Name, in Scripture, the authority or character of a person. Where two or three are gathered together in my name, Matthew 18:20, Christ's promise to the assembly acting under His authority.
webster_full: Gather, to bring together; to collect individuals into one body or place.
Name, in Scripture, the authority, character, or revealed person of one named.
Greek synagō, to gather together, whence synagogue, an assembly.
Greek eis to emon onoma, unto my name — by His authority, not merely with mention of it.
Set at the close of the rule for church discipline, Matthew 18:15-20.
scriptures: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven.
And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: The promise is detached from the church and its discipline and made a guarantee attaching to any small gathering, which is then used to argue that no congregation is needed at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern use of the verse is almost always as an assurance to a handful of friends that Christ is present wherever a few meet — and from there to the conclusion that formal church membership, ordinances, officers and discipline are optional extras for people who like institutions. Matthew 18 gives the words a precise home. They close a passage about telling a brother his fault, about witnesses, about the judgment of the church, and about binding and loosing; the two or three are the witnesses and the assembly of that very procedure. A text about the authority of the gathered church cannot be made an argument for dispensing with it.

The second misuse treats the words as a promise of felt presence proportioned to numbers, so that a small meeting must reassure itself. Christ's presence is not quantitative and the verse does not compare crowds. The principle to recover is the one the Reformed and baptist confessions draw out: the Lord Jesus is in the midst of His gathered people by His Spirit, so that a small congregation faithfully keeping His order lacks nothing of His authority — and, by the same token, the assembly that acts in His name must actually act in it, since the promise is to those gathered unto His name and not merely in His general vicinity.
roots_summary: Greek synagō, to gather, root of synagogue; eis to emon onoma, unto My name, that is, by His authority — set within the rule of church discipline.
roots_lines: Greek synagō (perfect passive), having been gathered together.
Greek duo ē treis, two or three — the witnesses of Matthew 18:16.
Greek onoma, name, standing for the authority and person named.
Greek en mesōi autōn, in the midst of them, of Christ's own presence.
Preceded by binding and loosing and the judgment of the church, Matthew 18:17-18.
usage: where two or three are gathered together in my name
there am I in the midst of them
tell it unto the church

word: By Their Fruits Ye Shall Know Them
pronunciation: by thair FROOTS yee shal NOH them
pos: n. phr. (Christ's test for false prophets at the close of the Sermon on the Mount)
etymology: Greek apo tōn karpōn autōn epignōsesthe autous — karpos, fruit; epiginōskō, to know thoroughly or recognise upon examination, a stronger verb than simple knowing.
biblical_def: The Sermon on the Mount ends with warnings, and the first concerns teachers: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. Ye shall know them by their fruits,” and again, “Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” The test is given because the wolves are disguised; if false teachers announced themselves no test would be needed. Fruit in this paragraph is not merely outward respectability, which the sheep's clothing supplies, and it is not success, since the next verses describe men who prophesied and cast out devils and are still told, I never knew you. The fruit of a teacher in Scripture is the doctrine he bears and the life it grows — the apostle's charge to Timothy joins sound doctrine and godly conduct and treats them as one fabric. The verb is worth marking: epiginōskō, to recognise on examination. Christ does not say that fruit is obvious at a glance; He commands an inspection, and the Bereans who searched the scriptures daily were doing exactly what He here requires. The Reformed have therefore used this verse against both a credulous charity that refuses to test anyone and a suspicious spirit that condemns without examining.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Fruit, the produce of a tree or plant; in Scripture, effect, consequence, or the product of a man's character. Know, to perceive with certainty; to recognise. By their fruits ye shall know them, Matthew 7:20, Christ's test for disguised false prophets.
webster_full: Fruit, the produce of a tree or plant; effect or consequence; product.
Know, to perceive with certainty; to recognise upon examination.
Greek karpos, fruit, whether of a tree or of a man's doctrine and life.
Greek epiginōskō, to know fully, to recognise after inspection.
Given against wolves in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15.
scriptures: Mat 7:20
Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.
Mat 7:16
Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?
Mat 7:21
Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
corruption_summary: The test is turned into pragmatism, where numbers and influence count as fruit, or else into a prohibition on judging at all, so that no teacher may be examined.
corruption_paragraphs: The pragmatic reading counts crowds, budgets, and reach as the fruit Christ meant, and so canonises whatever grows. The paragraph refuses it in the plainest possible way: the men dismissed in the following verses had prophesied, cast out devils, and done many wonderful works in His name, and the sentence on them is, I never knew you, depart from me, ye that work iniquity. Results on that scale are not the fruit in view. What the New Testament elsewhere names as fruit is the fruit of the Spirit in a man and the soundness of the doctrine he teaches, and a ministry may be large and bear neither.

The opposite error is now more common in the churches, where any examination of a teacher is met with judge not, that ye be not judged — from this very sermon, two chapters earlier. The Lord who forbade hypocritical judgment in chapter seven commands discriminating inspection in the same chapter, and the apostles follow Him, naming Hymenaeus, Alexander and Demas, marking those who cause divisions, and commending the Bereans for daily searching. The principle to recover is that charity and testing are not rivals: believe the best of men, and still try the spirits, because the clothing is sheep's and the appetite is a wolf's.
roots_summary: Greek karpos, fruit; epiginōskō, to recognise upon examination; pseudoprophētēs, false prophet — the test is given because the disguise is deliberate.
roots_lines: Greek karpos, fruit; the produce by which a tree's kind is known.
Greek epiginōskō, to know thoroughly, recognise on inspection.
Greek pseudoprophētēs, a false prophet, in sheep's clothing.
Greek harpax, ravening or rapacious, of the wolf's inward appetite.
Followed by those who did many wonderful works and were disowned, Matthew 7:22-23.

pos: n. phr. (the close of Christ's argument against anxious thought for the morrow)
etymology: Greek arketon tēi hēmerai hē kakia autēs — arketos, sufficient or enough; kakia, evil, here in the sense of trouble or hardship rather than wickedness.
biblical_def: “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” The Lord has been reasoning from the fowls of the air and the lilies of the field to the care of His Father for His own, and this is the conclusion. Note first what the phrase concedes. It does not say the day is free of evil; it says the day has enough of it. Christ grants the trouble and forbids the borrowing — a man is given grace sufficient for today's burden, and not for today's burden plus an imagined tomorrow. The old English “take no thought” has misled readers, for the Greek word is not thinking or planning but the divided, distracting care that pulls a man apart; Scripture elsewhere commends the ant that provides in summer and tells a man to count the cost before he builds. What is forbidden is the anxiety that acts as though the Father were absent from the morrow. The remedy Christ gives is not a technique but a redirection: seek ye first the kingdom of God, and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added. The order matters. Anxiety is cured by a greater object, not by reassurance about the lesser ones.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Sufficient, enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate. Evil, misfortune, calamity, injury, mischief. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof, Matthew 6:34, the day's own trouble is enough without borrowing tomorrow's.
webster_full: Sufficient, enough; adequate; equal to the end or purpose proposed.
Evil, misfortune, calamity, mischief; whatever is injurious or grievous.
Greek arketos, sufficient, enough, satisfying the measure.
Greek kakia, here trouble or hardship, not moral wickedness.
Greek merimnaō, to be drawn apart by care, rendered ‘take thought’.
scriptures: Mat 6:34
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
Mat 6:33
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Mat 6:25

Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?
Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
corruption_summary: The saying is read as a counsel of improvidence on one side and as a therapeutic mantra of living in the moment on the other, neither of which is the Father's care Christ is arguing from.
corruption_paragraphs: Read as a ban on planning, the verse is set against the plain commands of Scripture elsewhere: the ant provideth her meat in the summer, the prudent man foreseeth the evil, a builder counts the cost, and Joseph stored grain for seven years of famine by God's own direction. The Greek verb is merimnaō, to be pulled apart with care, and the archaic “take no thought” must be read in that sense or the Bible contradicts itself. A Christian may buy insurance, keep a budget and plant a field; what he may not do is carry tomorrow as though he had no Father.

The therapeutic reading is now the more common. Mindfulness literature and its Christian imitations quote the verse as present-moment awareness, a practice of attention that calms the nervous system — and the Father drops out of the sentence altogether. Christ's whole argument is His Father's care: your heavenly Father feedeth the fowls, clotheth the grass, knoweth that ye have need of these things. Strip that out and nothing remains but a mood. The principle to recover is the order of the preceding verse: anxiety is answered by seeking first the kingdom of God, which is to say by having a greater treasure than the one that is threatened.
roots_summary: Greek arketos, sufficient; kakia, trouble; merimnaō, to be drawn apart by care — the day's evil is granted, and the borrowing of tomorrow's is forbidden.

word: Seek Ye First the Kingdom of God
pronunciation: SEEK yee FURST thuh KING-dum uv GOD
pos: v. phr. (Christ's positive command against anxiety, with its attached promise)
etymology: Greek zēteite de prōton tēn basileian tou theou — zēteō, to seek, in the present imperative of continued action; prōton, first in order and in rank; basileia, kingdom or reign.
biblical_def: “But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.” This is the hinge of the Sermon's teaching on anxiety: having forbidden the care that distracts and reasoned from the Father's feeding of the birds, Christ now gives the positive command. Three things are exact in it. The seeking is continuous, a present imperative, not a decision made once. First is first in rank, not merely in sequence — the kingdom is not the earliest item on a list that later gets to food and clothing, but the one pursuit everything else is ordered under. And the object is twofold: the kingdom of God and his righteousness, which forbids any seeking of the reign without the holiness that belongs to it. The attached promise is as carefully worded as the command. These things shall be added — added, as an appendage to something greater, and these things means what the paragraph has named, food, drink and clothing, the Father's provision for His children's need. The Lord does not promise abundance; He promises that the man who makes God's reign his business will not be abandoned in the matter of his bread. That is why the same Sermon teaches a disciple to pray for daily bread and no more.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Seek, to go in search of; to look for; to make inquiry after. Kingdom, the territory or people subject to a king; the reign of God in the heart and over His people. Seek ye first the kingdom of God, Matthew 6:33, the positive command answering anxious care.
webster_full: Seek, to go in search of; to look for; to endeavour to find or gain.
Kingdom, the dominion of a king; in Scripture, the reign and rule of God.
Greek zēteō, to seek, here in the present imperative of continued action.
Greek prōton, first; first in rank and order of importance.
Greek prostithēmi, to add to, of the things promised besides.
scriptures: Mat 6:33
But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Mat 6:32
(For after all these things do the Gentiles seek:) for your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.
But rather seek ye the kingdom of God; and all these things shall be added unto you.
Col 3:1
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God.
corruption_summary: The promise is detached from the command and sold as a formula for prosperity, while the words “and his righteousness” are commonly dropped altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity preachers' use of this verse keeps the promise and loses the object: seek the kingdom as a means, and the all-these-things follow as wealth. Two words block it. The first is added — what is added is an appendage, not the point, and the paragraph has already told us what it covers, which is food, drink and raiment. The second is righteousness, almost universally omitted in the formula, because a kingdom sought together with God's righteousness cannot be sought as a technique for gain. Paul's warning to Timothy about those supposing that gain is godliness answers the whole scheme, and his own learned contentment in whatsoever state answers it again.

A second and subtler failure keeps the command but makes the kingdom a private interior experience, so that seeking it first costs nothing visible in a man's calendar or purse. Christ's own measures are concrete: where a man's treasure is, there is his heart; no man can serve God and mammon; lay up treasure in heaven. The principle to recover is that first means first in fact. A life in which the kingdom is sought first will show it in what is given away, what is refused, and what is risked, and the promise of provision is spoken to such a life and not to a sentiment about it.
roots_summary: Greek zēteō, to seek, present imperative; prōton, first in rank; dikaiosynē, righteousness, joined to the kingdom as a second object of the same seeking.

word: To Day Shalt Thou Be With Me in Paradise
pronunciation: too-DAY shalt thow bee with MEE in PAR-uh-dys
pos: n. phr. (Christ's word from the cross to the believing thief)
etymology: Greek sēmeron met emou esēi en tōi paradeisōi — sēmeron, today; paradeisos, a word of Persian origin for a walled garden or park, used in the Greek Old Testament of Eden and in the New of the place of the blessed dead.
biblical_def: One of the two malefactors crucified with Christ railed; the other rebuked him, confessed the justice of his own sentence, owned Christ's innocence, and asked, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. “And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” Few verses carry so much doctrine in so few words. The man is saved by faith alone, with no time left for any work: he is not baptised, performs no restitution, joins no assembly, and dies a criminal justly condemned — and he is promised paradise that same day. He asked to be remembered at a future coming and was answered with today, which tells us that the soul of a believer passes at death immediately into blessedness and does not sleep or wait. And the promise is with me: paradise is defined by the presence of Christ, not by its furniture. The apostle's desire to depart and be with Christ, and his confidence that to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord, say exactly what this verse says. The Reformed confessions rest the intermediate state here, and so does every deathbed hope of a sinner converted late.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Paradise, the garden of Eden; the blissful regions where the souls of the righteous dwell after death. To day, on this day; at the present time. To day shalt thou be with me in paradise, Luke 23:43, Christ's promise to the believing thief.
webster_full: Paradise, the garden of Eden; the blissful seat of the souls of the righteous.
To day, on this very day; at the present time, without delay.
Greek paradeisos, a walled garden or park; used of Eden in the Septuagint.
Greek sēmeron, today — answering a request about a future coming.
Named again of the third heaven, 2 Corinthians 12:4, and Revelation 2:7.
scriptures: And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
Php 1:23
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
corruption_summary: The verse is evaded by repunctuation, by soul-sleep, and by purgatory, each of which must remove either the “today” or the “with me” that the sentence actually contains.
corruption_paragraphs: The best-known evasion is a comma. Watchtower publications and others who deny the conscious intermediate state move the punctuation to read, Verily I say unto thee today, shalt thou be with me in paradise — making today modify the saying rather than the arrival. The device fails on the Lord's own idiom, which is Verily I say unto thee some seventy times without a day attached, since the day a thing is said needs no stating; and it leaves the word doing nothing at all in a sentence that was plainly framed to answer a question about a distant kingdom with an immediate promise. Soul-sleep requires the same surgery, for a sleeping soul is not with anyone.

Rome's purgatory must blunt the verse from the other side. On that scheme a justly condemned criminal, converted in his last hour with no satisfaction made and no temporal punishment discharged, would be the clearest possible candidate for a long purging. Christ promises him paradise the same day. The principle to recover is justification by faith alone with nothing added: the thief had faith, a true repentance confessing the justice of his sentence, and no works whatever, and the dying Saviour gave him His own company that afternoon. Every doctrine of after-death satisfaction stands condemned by the one sentence Christ spoke to a man who had no time to satisfy anything.
roots_summary: Greek paradeisos, a walled garden, used of Eden and of the abode of the blessed dead; sēmeron, today — an immediate answer to a question about a future kingdom.

Greek mnēsthēti mou, remember me, the thief's own request.
